story: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira, in northern Greece. His father was the doctor to the king of Macedon.
At 17 he went to Athens to study at Plato's Academy, the best school in the Greek world, and stayed for about 20 years.
After Plato died, he travelled. On the island of Lesbos he studied sea creatures up close, one of the first people to do science by careful watching.
In 343 BC King Philip asked him to teach his son, the future Alexander the Great.
Back in Athens he opened his own school, the Lyceum. He wrote about almost everything: logic, animals, the stars, politics, poetry and how to live a good life.
He left Athens in 323 BC, when feeling turned against anyone linked to Macedon, and died the next year.

story: Alexander was born in 356 BC in Macedon, in northern Greece, the son of King Philip II, who had built the strongest army of the time.
From 13 to 16 he was taught by the philosopher Aristotle. He loved Homer's Iliad and dreamed of being a hero like Achilles.
His father was murdered in 336 BC, and Alexander became king at 20. Two years later he crossed into Asia to take on the huge Persian Empire.
He beat the Persians at the Granicus river, at Issus and finally at Gaugamela in 331 BC, took Egypt (where he founded the city of Alexandria), and pushed on as far as India.
In India his exhausted army refused to go further, and he had to turn back. He died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32, and his generals split his empire between them.

story: Napoleon was born in 1769 on Corsica, an island France had taken over the year before. At nine he was sent to a military school in France, where other boys mocked his accent and his family's lack of money. He spent his free time reading history.

He became an artillery officer. In 1793, aged 24, he worked out how to drive the British fleet out of the port of Toulon: take the hills above the harbor and put cannons there. It worked, and he was made a general.
In 1796 he was given France's army in Italy: hungry, unpaid and losing. Within months he won battle after battle, mostly by moving faster than his enemies and hitting them one at a time.
In 1799 he seized power, and in 1804 he crowned himself Emperor. He also rewrote France's laws into one clear code, the Napoleonic Code, which is still the base of the law in many countries.
His greatest win was Austerlitz in 1805. Then he overreached: a long war in Spain, and in 1812 an invasion of Russia that cost him most of his army.
He was exiled in 1814, escaped and came back for 100 days, and lost for good at Waterloo in 1815. He died in exile on the island of Saint Helena in 1821.

text: Like Napoleon, Elon Musk is known for very long working weeks, getting into the smallest details himself, and deadlines that most people think are impossible.

Both stories also show the risk: taking on too much at once.
thenNow.trading: Speed and hands-on work win, but only with a limit you respect. Plan fast, act fast, and stop for the day when you hit your loss limit.

story: Julius Caesar was born in 100 BC into an old Roman family that had more name than money.
As a young man he was captured by pirates. He joked with them, wrote poems while he waited for the ransom, and told them he'd come back and punish them. He did.
He climbed Rome's political ladder by spending huge sums on games and favors, borrowing heavily, and making a deal with Rome's two most powerful men, Pompey and Crassus.
From 58 to 50 BC he conquered Gaul (roughly today's France and Belgium) and wrote short, clear reports on the war that are still read today.

In 49 BC he crossed the Rubicon river with his army, starting a civil war, and won it. He made himself dictator, and among many reforms he fixed the calendar: our 365-day year with a leap day comes from him.
Many senators feared he would make himself king, and on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BC a group of them stabbed him to death.

carried.title: Mercy as a strategy

carried.source: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar, ch. 75

Buy double to make up for being late
task.why: Haste makes waste.

quotes.text: Remember that time is money.
quotes.source: Advice to a Young Tradesman, 1748
quotes.plain: Time you waste is money you could have made.
quotes.trading: Spend your trading time on planning and review, not on staring at the screen.

quotes.text: Money can beget money, and its offspring can beget more, and so on.
quotes.source: Advice to a Young Tradesman, 1748
quotes.plain: Money you keep and invest earns more money, and then that earns more too.
quotes.trading: Protect your account first. A big loss stops your money from growing.

quotes.text: Lost time is never found again.
quotes.source: Poor Richard's Almanack, 1748
quotes.plain: You can't get back time you wasted.
quotes.trading: Learn from every loss right away, so the time it cost you isn't wasted.

quotes.text: Well done is better than well said.
quotes.source: Poor Richard's Almanack, 1737
quotes.plain: Doing something matters more than talking about it.
quotes.trading: Talking about trades is easy. Follow your plan in your account; that's what counts.

story: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706, the 15th of 17 children. His family could only afford two years of school.
At 12 he started work in his brother's print shop. At 17 he ran away to Philadelphia with almost no money and no friends there.
He built his own printing business with long hours and a reputation for being reliable. His yearly book of advice, Poor Richard's Almanack, made him famous.

At 42 he had enough money to step back from business, and spent his time on science and his city: he proved lightning is electricity, invented the lightning rod and bifocal glasses, and started a library, a fire company and a university.
He then became a diplomat. In Paris he won France to America's side in its war for independence, and he signed both the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution.
He died in 1790, one of the most famous people in the world.

carried.title: He taught himself to write
carried.text: Without schooling, he took essays he admired, wrote them out again from memory, then compared his version with the original to find his mistakes.
carried.source: Franklin, Autobiography

carried.title: He let people see the work
carried.text: As a young printer he made a point of being seen working, and sometimes pushed his own paper home through the streets in a wheelbarrow, so people knew he was hardworking and could be trusted.
carried.source: Franklin, Autobiography

carried.title: A club for getting better
carried.text: At 21 he started the Junto, a weekly club of young tradesmen who met to swap ideas, books and advice on improving themselves and their city.
carried.source: Franklin, Autobiography

studied.title: Books
studied.text: Franklin taught himself from the books he could borrow or buy: Plutarch's Lives, Bunyan, and Defoe's Essay upon Projects, which he said shaped how he thought.

text: Warren Buffett, like Franklin, explains money in plain words. His yearly letters to his shareholders are read almost like Poor Richard's Almanack.
Both made most of their fortune by letting money grow on itself over a very long time, and both are known for simple, careful habits.
thenNow.trading: Compounding needs time and no big losses. Protect your account first; growth comes from staying in the game.

story.credit: Benjamin West, Benjamin Franklin Drawing Electricity from the Sky (about 1816), Philadelphia Museum of Art. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

carried.credit: Franklin's chart for his 13 virtues, redrawn from his Autobiography. Public domain (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons.

figures.name: Thomas Edison
figures.tagline: The inventor of the phonograph and a practical light bulb, who built the first invention factory.

lessons.title: Ninety-nine percent work
text: Edison said genius is mostly hard work, not a flash of brilliance.
His lab tested thousands of materials to find a light bulb filament that lasted.
lessons.trading: There is no magic setup. Steady practice, review and patience make a trader.

lessons.title: Every miss is information
text: When a helper felt sorry about thousands of failed tests, Edison said he had lots of results: he now knew thousands of things that didn't work.
A failed test is still a result.
lessons.trading: A losing trade that followed your rules isn't a failure. It's data. Write down what happened and keep going.

lessons.title: Build a system
text: At Menlo Park, Edison built a lab where a team invented things on a schedule. It was the first invention factory.
He turned invention from luck into a process.
lessons.trading: Turn trading into a routine: scan, plan, enter, manage, review. A process you repeat beats waiting for inspiration.

lessons.title: Make it useful
text: Edison aimed his lab at inventions people would actually buy and use: light, sound recording, movies.
Clever doesn't count if nobody can use it.
lessons.trading: Use tools you understand. A simple strategy you follow is worth more than a complicated one you don't.

quotes.text: Genius is one per cent inspiration, ninety-nine per cent perspiration.
quotes.source: Thomas Edison, spoken c. 1903 (as published in Harper's Monthly, September 1932)
quotes.plain: Success comes mostly from hard work, not from being a genius.
quotes.trading: Show up, follow the plan, review. That's the 99%.

quotes.text: Why, man, I have gotten lots of results! I know several thousand things that won't work.
quotes.source: Frank Dyer and T. C. Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions (1910), as remembered by his associate Walter Mallory
quotes.plain: Each failure taught him something, so none of them was wasted.
quotes.trading: Every losing trade teaches you something, if you write it down.

story: Thomas Edison was born in Ohio in 1847. He had only a few months of school and was taught mostly by his mother.
At 12 he sold newspapers and snacks on trains, and set up a little chemistry lab in a baggage car. He lost most of his hearing as a boy.
He became a telegraph operator, then an inventor. His first patent, a machine to count votes, didn't sell: nobody wanted it. He decided to only invent things people would pay for.
In 1876 he built a laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, with a team that invented on purpose, day after day.
Out came the phonograph (1877), a long-lasting light bulb (1879) and the whole system to power it: in 1882 his Pearl Street station began lighting part of New York. Later came early movie cameras.
He collected 1,093 US patents and died in 1931.

carried.title: Learn from the first flop
carried.text: When his first invention, a vote-counting machine, found no buyers, he decided never again to invent something nobody wanted.
carried.source: Frank Dyer and T. C. Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions (1910)

carried.title: Work beside the team
carried.text: He worked through the night with his team at Menlo Park and was known to nap on a lab bench or a table before carrying on.
carried.source: Frank Dyer and T. C. Martin, Edison: His Life and Inventions (1910)

carried.title: Calm in a disaster
carried.text: When fire destroyed much of his factory in 1914, his son recalled him calmly watching it and saying they could rebuild. Work started again the next day.
carried.source: As recalled by his son Charles Edison; told in Edmund Morris, Edison (2019)

studied.title: His rival, Tesla
studied.text: Edison employed the young Tesla for a few months. Their rivalry, Edison's DC against Tesla's AC, became known as the 'war of the currents'.
studied.source: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla: Inventor of the Electrical Age (2013)

text: Steve Jobs, like Edison, was less a lone inventor than a builder of teams and products that ordinary people wanted.
Edison sold a whole system (the bulb and the power to run it); Apple sold the device, the software and the store together.
thenNow.trading: Think in systems, not single tricks: your setup, your sizing, your exits and your review all work together.

story.credit: Thomas Edison with his phonograph, photographed at Mathew Brady's studio (1878), Library of Congress. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

carried.credit: Edison's laboratory at Menlo Park and its team (1879), Thomas Edison National Historical Park. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

figures.name: Nikola Tesla
figures.tagline: The inventor of the AC power system that lights the world, who built machines in his head first.

lessons.title: Build it in your head first
text: Tesla said he didn't rush to build. He pictured each machine in his mind, ran it, and fixed it there before touching any metal.
Thinking first saved him months of trial and error.
lessons.trading: Picture the trade before you take it: where you get in, where you're wrong, where you take profit. If you can't see it clearly, don't take it.

lessons.title: A little theory saves a lot of work
text: Tesla once worked for Edison. He felt Edison tried things blindly, when a little math would have saved most of the effort.
Understanding why beats guessing.
lessons.trading: Learn why a setup works (trend, support, volume), not just what it looks like. Then you can spot when it won't work.

lessons.title: Think long term
text: Tesla's AC power won the 'war of the currents' against Edison's DC system and still powers homes today. He kept looking decades ahead.
Big ideas take time to pay off.
lessons.trading: Not every idea is a day trade. The Long-term section of Market is for ideas that need weeks or months to work.

lessons.title: Deep focus
text: Tesla worked long hours alone, deep in one problem at a time.
Big breakthroughs need long stretches without distraction.
lessons.trading: Turn off what distracts you when you study charts. One focused hour beats a whole day half-watching.

quotes.text: My method is different. I do not rush into actual work. When I get an idea I start at once building it up in my imagination.
quotes.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919), ch. 1
quotes.plain: He planned everything in his head before doing it for real.
quotes.trading: Plan the whole trade before you click Buy.

quotes.text: The progressive development of man is vitally dependent on invention.
quotes.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919), opening line
quotes.plain: People move forward by inventing new things.
quotes.trading: Keep improving your method. What worked last year may need a tweak this year.

quotes.text: If Edison had a needle to find in a haystack, he would proceed at once with the diligence of the bee to examine straw after straw until he found the object of his search.
quotes.source: Nikola Tesla, quoted in The New York Times, 19 October 1931
quotes.plain: Edison worked very hard, but often by brute force instead of thinking first.
quotes.trading: Don't test random ideas on real money. Think first, then test with practice money.

story: Nikola Tesla was born in 1856 in a Serbian family in Smiljan, in today's Croatia. He studied engineering in Austria.
In 1882, walking in a park in Budapest, he suddenly saw how to build a motor run by alternating current (AC), a type of electricity that can travel much further than Edison's DC.
In 1884 he arrived in New York with almost nothing and worked for Edison for a few months, before leaving after a dispute.
After his first company pushed him out, he dug ditches for a living for a while. Then his AC patents were bought by George Westinghouse.
AC won the 'war of the currents', and in 1895 his system powered the great Niagara Falls power station. He went on to work on radio and wireless power.
He was brilliant but bad with money. His big wireless tower project ran out of funding, and he died alone and poor in a New York hotel room in 1943.

carried.title: The idea in the park
carried.text: Walking in Budapest and reciting a poem, he suddenly saw how his AC motor would work, and drew the design in the sand with a stick.
carried.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919)

carried.title: Down but not out
carried.text: After his first company pushed him out, he dug ditches for a living. Within about two years, his AC patents were being bought by Westinghouse.
carried.source: W. Bernard Carlson, Tesla: Inventor of the Electrical Age (2013)

carried.title: Running it all in his head
carried.text: He said he could picture a machine so exactly in his mind that he could see which parts would wear out, before building anything.
carried.source: Nikola Tesla, My Inventions (1919)

studied.title: Edison
studied.text: Tesla came to America with a letter of introduction to Edison and worked for him for a few months. They split over money and over AC versus DC, and became famous rivals.

thenNow.modern: the car company named after him
text: The best-known car company of our time was named after Nikola Tesla when it was founded in 2003, more than 50 years after he died poor.
His ideas paid off hugely, but mostly for others, because he never learned to protect and fund his own work.
thenNow.trading: A great idea isn't enough. In trading, a great entry is wasted without a stop and a plan for taking profit.

story.credit: Tesla's Colorado Springs laboratory, photograph by Charles Alley (1899). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

carried.credit: Nikola Tesla in his Colorado Springs laboratory, photograph by Dickenson V. Alley (1899, a double exposure). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

figures.name: Jesse Livermore
figures.tagline: The most famous stock trader ever: made and lost several fortunes, and made millions betting against the 1929 crash.

lessons.title: Follow the line of least resistance
text: Livermore believed prices move in the easiest direction, like water running downhill, and keep going until something stops them.
He didn't try to guess tops and bottoms. He waited for the market to show its direction, then went with it.
lessons.trading: Trade with the trend, not against it. If a stock keeps making higher highs and higher lows, don't keep shorting it because it 'must' fall.

lessons.title: The money is in the sitting
text: He said his big profits never came from clever thinking. They came from sitting tight in a winning trade while the move played out.
Most people take a small profit too early, and hold their losers too long.
lessons.trading: Let winners run with a trailing stop. Cut losers fast at your stop. Most beginners do the opposite.

lessons.title: Keep a notebook
text: As a teenage clerk writing prices on a board, he kept a notebook of how prices moved before big changes, and tested his guesses on paper before risking a cent.
His 'feel' for the market came from years of written records.
lessons.trading: Journal every trade and every pattern you notice. Your notes become your edge.

lessons.title: Even the best go broke
text: Livermore went broke more than once: by trading too big, trusting tips and breaking his own rules.
Each comeback started with admitting exactly what he'd done wrong.
lessons.trading: Never risk so much that one bad run wipes you out. Small, fixed risk per trade keeps you in the game.

quotes.text: There is nothing new in Wall Street. There can't be because speculation is as old as the hills. Whatever happens in the stock market today has happened before and will happen again.
quotes.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923), ch. 1: the thinly disguised story of Livermore's life, told in his voice
quotes.plain: Markets go up and down for the same human reasons they always have: greed and fear.
quotes.trading: Study old charts. The patterns repeat because people don't change.

quotes.text: It never was my thinking that made the big money for me. It always was my sitting.
quotes.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923), ch. 5
quotes.plain: His profits came from holding good trades long enough, not from being clever.
quotes.trading: Once a trade works, don't rush out. Let it run with a stop that follows it.

quotes.text: Prices, like everything else, move along the line of least resistance.
quotes.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)
quotes.plain: Prices go the easy way, like water going downhill.
quotes.trading: Trade in the direction the stock is already going.

quotes.text: The game taught me the game. And it didn't spare the rod while teaching.
quotes.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)
quotes.plain: He learned by losing, and the lessons hurt.
quotes.trading: Practice money lets you learn the lessons without the pain. Use it.

story: Jesse Livermore was born on a poor farm in Massachusetts in 1877. At 14 he left home with five dollars and found a job in Boston writing stock prices on a big board at a brokerage.
Writing the same prices all day, he started noticing patterns, and wrote them in a notebook.
He began betting on prices in 'bucket shops', betting parlors on stock prices, and won so often that they banned him. People called him the 'Boy Plunger'.
In New York he made and lost fortunes. In 1906 he was betting against Union Pacific stock when the San Francisco earthquake hit, and the fall made him rich.
In the panic of 1907 he made about a million dollars in a day, and in the 1929 crash he made millions more by betting prices would fall.
His last years were hard: he lost most of his fortune, and died in 1940. His story is still the book traders recommend most.

carried.title: He wrote it all down
carried.text: As a teenage board boy, he kept a little notebook of how prices moved before big changes, and 'traded' his guesses on paper long before he used real money.
carried.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923), ch. 1

carried.title: Banned for winning
carried.text: He won so often in the bucket shops of Boston that they refused to take his bets, so he had to trade under other names and then move to New York.
carried.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)

carried.title: Owning his mistakes
carried.text: Each time he went broke, he went back over exactly which rule he'd broken: trading too big, acting on tips, or not waiting for the right moment.
carried.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)

carried.title: When Morgan asked
carried.text: In the 1907 panic, with prices collapsing, he was asked on behalf of J.P. Morgan's circle to stop betting against the market. He agreed, covered, and bought stocks near the bottom instead.
carried.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)

studied.title: J.P. Morgan
studied.text: In the 1907 panic, Livermore stopped betting against the market when Morgan's circle asked him to, and bought instead.
studied.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)

story.credit: A crowd on Wall Street in the Panic of 1907, New York Public Library. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

carried.credit: The floor of the New York Stock Exchange, by Helen D. Van Eaton, Leslie's Monthly Magazine (1908). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

figures.name: Charles Dow
figures.tagline: Founder of The Wall Street Journal and the Dow average, whose ideas about trends started chart reading.

lessons.title: Measure the whole market
text: In 1884 Dow simply added up the prices of 11 big stocks, mostly railroads, and divided by the number. It was the first stock market average.
One number showed whether the market as a whole was rising or falling.
lessons.trading: Before trading a stock, check the market. Most stocks follow SPY and QQQ; swimming against the whole market is hard.

lessons.title: Tides, waves and ripples
text: Dow wrote that the market has three movements at once: the big main trend that lasts years, shorter swings of weeks, and small day-to-day moves.
He compared them to the tide, the waves and the ripples on a beach.
lessons.trading: Know which one you're trading. A day trader rides ripples, a swing trader waves, a long-term investor the tide. Check the bigger trend before you enter.

lessons.title: Look for confirmation
text: Dow and those who carried on his ideas watched for the industrial and railroad averages to move together. One alone could be a false signal; both together meant a real trend.
One clue is a hint. Two clues that agree are evidence.
lessons.trading: Don't trade on one signal. Look for price, volume and the market's direction to agree.

lessons.title: Report, don't guess
text: Dow was a reporter first. His paper's job was to give traders fast, accurate facts, not tips.
He built his reputation on being careful and correct.
lessons.trading: Separate facts (price, volume, earnings) from opinions (tips, hype). Trade the facts.

quotes.text: The market is always to be considered as having three movements, all going at the same time.
quotes.source: Charles Dow, The Wall Street Journal (editorial, 1902), as collected in S. A. Nelson, The ABC of Stock Speculation (1902)
quotes.plain: Big trend, medium swings and small daily moves all happen at once.
quotes.trading: Check the big trend before you trade the small move.

quotes.text: A person watching the tide coming in and who wishes to know the exact spot which marks the high tide, sets a stick in the sand at the points reached by the incoming waves until the stick reaches a position where the waves do not come up to it.
quotes.source: Charles Dow, The Wall Street Journal (editorial, 1900), as collected in S. A. Nelson, The ABC of Stock Speculation (1902)
quotes.plain: You find out the tide has turned when the waves stop reaching your marker.
quotes.trading: A trend is over when price stops making new highs. Mark the last high, and watch whether it's beaten.

story: Charles Dow was born on a farm in Connecticut in 1851. He left school young and became a newspaper reporter.
In 1880 he moved to New York to report on Wall Street. Two years later he and Edward Jones started Dow Jones & Company, delivering short handwritten news bulletins to traders.
In 1884 he published the first stock market average, and in 1889 the company launched The Wall Street Journal.
In 1896 he started the Dow Jones Industrial Average with 12 companies. It still exists, now with 30.
In his editorials he explained how the market moves in trends. After he died in 1902, others collected these ideas and called them 'Dow Theory', the start of technical analysis.

carried.title: News, fast
carried.text: Dow Jones started by sending messengers around Wall Street with short handwritten news sheets, so traders got facts quickly.
carried.source: Dow Jones & Company history; Wall Street Journal archives

carried.title: Simple tools
carried.text: His first average was nothing fancy: add up the prices of a few big stocks and divide. Simple enough that anyone could follow it.
carried.source: The Wall Street Journal; S. A. Nelson, The ABC of Stock Speculation (1902)

carried.title: A careful writer
carried.text: He wrote short, plain editorials explaining what the market was doing and why, rather than predicting or promoting stocks.
carried.source: S. A. Nelson, The ABC of Stock Speculation (1902)

studied.title: Those who came after
studied.text: After Dow died, his ideas were collected and named 'Dow Theory', and nearly every chart method since builds on them.
studied.source: S. A. Nelson, The ABC of Stock Speculation (1902); W. P. Hamilton, The Stock Market Barometer (1922)

story.credit: The first issue of The Wall Street Journal (8 July 1889), Dow Jones & Company. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

carried.credit: Thomas Edison's stock ticker, National Museum of American History, photograph by Jaclyn Nash. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

figures.name: Isaac Newton
figures.tagline: The genius who explained gravity, and then lost a fortune in a stock market bubble.

lessons.title: Even a genius can catch the fever
text: In 1720 shares in the South Sea Company soared. Newton bought, sold early with a good profit, then watched the price keep climbing without him.
He bought back in, much higher, just before the crash, and lost a fortune.
lessons.trading: Missing a move is not a loss. Chasing it is how you buy the top. If you missed it, wait for the next setup.

lessons.title: Stand on giants' shoulders
text: Newton built on the work of Galileo, Kepler and others before him, and said so.
Even the greatest mind of his age started by studying the best who came before.
lessons.trading: Learn proven methods first, then improve on them.

lessons.title: Test it, don't just believe it
text: Newton built his ideas on careful measurements and experiments, not on guesses. He wrote that he did not 'frame hypotheses' he couldn't support.
If the evidence didn't fit, the idea had to go.
lessons.trading: Back up your strategy with evidence: test it on old charts and with practice money before trusting it.

lessons.title: Deep work
text: When Cambridge closed during the plague of 1665–66, Newton went home and, mostly alone, worked out the beginnings of calculus, his ideas on light and on gravity.
Long, uninterrupted focus produced his biggest breakthroughs.
lessons.trading: Give your learning real, focused time. A distracted hour on the charts teaches little.

quotes.text: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.
quotes.source: Isaac Newton, letter to Robert Hooke, 5 February 1676
quotes.plain: He could see so far only because he built on the work of the great people before him.
quotes.trading: Study the traders and methods that came before you; you don't have to start from zero.

quotes.text: I frame no hypotheses.
quotes.source: Isaac Newton, Principia, General Scholium (2nd edition, 1713)
quotes.plain: He refused to claim things he couldn't prove.
quotes.trading: Don't trade on a story you can't check. Trade what the chart and the numbers show.

story: Isaac Newton was born in 1643 in Lincolnshire, England. His father had died before he was born.
He studied at Cambridge. When the plague closed the university in 1665, he went home and, in about two years, laid the foundations of calculus, optics and his theory of gravity.
In 1687 he published the Principia, which explained gravity and how planets move. It made him the most famous scientist in the world.
In 1696 he went to run the Royal Mint, where he chased down forgers of coins.
In 1720, the South Sea Company bubble pulled in almost everyone in London. Newton made money, sold, bought back near the top, and lost heavily when it crashed.
He died in 1727, honored as one of the greatest minds who ever lived.

carried.title: Alone with a problem
carried.text: During the plague years, he worked mostly alone at his family's farm, thinking about one problem for days on end. That is where his ideas on gravity began.
carried.source: Richard Westfall, Never at Rest (1980)

carried.title: Forgetting to eat
carried.text: His assistant later remembered Newton so absorbed in his work that he forgot meals and often left food untouched.
carried.source: Recollections of Humphrey Newton, in letters to John Conduitt (1727–28)

carried.title: Detective at the Mint
carried.text: At the Mint he gathered evidence himself against coin forgers, questioning witnesses, and caught the notorious forger William Chaloner.
carried.source: Thomas Levenson, Newton and the Counterfeiter (2009)

carried.title: The bubble
carried.text: Records of his investments show he sold South Sea shares at a profit, bought back much higher, and lost a large part of his fortune in the crash.
carried.source: Andrew Odlyzko, 'Newton's financial misadventures in the South Sea Bubble' (2019)

studied.title: Galileo and Kepler
studied.text: Newton built his laws of motion and gravity on the work of Galileo and Kepler before him, and said he had seen further by standing on the shoulders of giants.
studied.source: Isaac Newton, letter to Robert Hooke, 1676

story.credit: The title page of Newton's Principia (1687), first edition, University of Strasbourg library. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

carried.credit: William Blake, Newton (about 1795–1805). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

figures.name: J.P. Morgan
figures.tagline: The banker who built giant companies and, at 70, stopped the Panic of 1907 almost single-handedly.

lessons.title: Calm in a crash
text: In October 1907 banks were failing and people were queuing to pull out their money. Morgan, 70 years old, took charge.
He sorted the banks that could be saved from those that couldn't, and organized the money to save them.
lessons.trading: Panic sells at the bottom. Have your plan (stops, position size) ready before the market gets wild, so you act instead of panic.

lessons.title: Character first
text: Asked by Congress whether loans were based on money or property, Morgan said the first thing was character.
He lent to people he trusted, and stayed away from those he didn't, however rich.
lessons.trading: Your discipline is your 'character' as a trader: doing what your plan says, every time.

lessons.title: Think big, organize well
text: Morgan reorganized failing railroads and in 1901 merged steel companies into U.S. Steel, the first company worth over a billion dollars.
He made messy industries simple and stable.
lessons.trading: Organize your trading: a clear watchlist, a routine and simple rules beat a messy screen full of ideas.

lessons.title: Cash is a weapon
text: Morgan could stop the panic because he and his friends had cash when everyone else was desperate for it.
In a crash, whoever has cash has choices.
lessons.trading: Keep some buying power free. After a sharp drop, the best setups need cash you didn't already spend.

quotes.text: The first thing is character.
quotes.source: J.P. Morgan, testimony to Congress (the Pujo Committee), 19 December 1912
quotes.plain: Trust in a person matters more than how much money they have.
quotes.trading: Your discipline matters more than the size of your account.

quotes.text: Before money or anything else. Money cannot buy it.
quotes.source: J.P. Morgan, testimony to Congress (the Pujo Committee), 19 December 1912, on character
quotes.plain: Good character comes first, and you can't buy it.
quotes.trading: Nobody can sell you discipline. You build it trade by trade.

story: John Pierpont Morgan was born in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1837, into a wealthy banking family. He studied in Switzerland and Germany.
He went into banking and became the most powerful banker in America, funding and reorganizing railroads.
In 1895, when the US government was running out of gold, his bank arranged the gold to steady it.
In 1901 he merged steel companies into U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar company.
In 1907 a panic swept the banks. Morgan, then 70, led the rescue. The scare led Congress to create the Federal Reserve in 1913, the same year he died.

carried.title: Locked in the library
carried.text: In November 1907, he gathered the leading bankers in his library in New York and, the story goes, locked the door until they agreed to put up the money to save the weaker banks.
carried.source: Jean Strouse, Morgan: American Financier (1999)

carried.title: Fast decisions
carried.text: During the panic he had experts check which banks were really sound, then decided in minutes who would be saved.
carried.source: Jean Strouse, Morgan: American Financier (1999)

carried.title: Character over money
carried.text: He told Congress he'd refuse to lend to a man he didn't trust, even with all the bonds in Christendom as security.
carried.source: J.P. Morgan, testimony to the Pujo Committee, 19 December 1912

studied.title: A trader in the panic
studied.text: In 1907, Morgan's circle asked the famous trader Jesse Livermore to stop betting against the market while they steadied it. He did.
studied.source: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923)
